question.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}+3{y}^{′}+(1+x)y=0.
$$

Suppose ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are solutions and their Wronskian $W(x)$ satisfies $W(2)=5.$ What is $W(6)?$

$W(6)=$ {{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
Abel's identity says that if ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are solutions of

$$
{y}^{″}+P(x){y}^{′}+Q(x)y=0,
$$

then their Wronskian $W(x)$ satisfies

$$
{W}^{′}(x)=-P(x)W(x).
$$

In our equation, the coefficient of ${y}^{′}$ is 

$$
P(x)=3.
$$

Substituting into Abel's identity gives

$$
{W}^{′}(x)=-3W(x).
$$

Now, we solve the first-order differential equation for $W:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{W}^{′} & =-3W \\ \frac{\text{d}W}{W} & =-3\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{\text{d}W}{W} & =\int -3\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|W| & =-3x+K \\ |W| & ={e}^{K}{e}^{-3x} \\ W & =C{e}^{-3x}\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Next, we use the given value $W(2)=5$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W(2) & =C{e}^{-3\cdot 2} \\ 5 & =C{e}^{-6} \\ C & =5{e}^{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
W(x)=5{e}^{6}{e}^{-3x}.
$$

Finally, we compute $W(6):$

$$
\begin{aligned}W(6) & =5{e}^{6}{e}^{-3\cdot 6}=5{e}^{-12}.\end{aligned}
$$
